Your first table
Today is your trial day at a restaurant. The head waiter has brought you into the dining room.
A family of two comes in through the door. What do you do?
I smile and greet them, ask if they have a reservation and take them to a table
The first 30 seconds set the tone for the guest's evening. The welcome must be quick and warm.
I'll see to them when I'm free, they're waiting anyway
A guest who goes unnoticed feels unimportant.
I say "Sit anywhere that's free" and go back to the kitchen
Taking guests to their table also keeps the dining room in order.

To the right of the plate

Above the plate

I say "Let me find out for you right away" and ask the chef

The dining room's order
Service station
A small store in the dining room. Spare cutlery, napkins, condiment sets and glasses are kept here; it is stocked before service starts.
service station
Condiment set
Salt shaker, pepper shaker and similar table items. They must be full, clean and the same on every table.
condiment set
Cutlery
Forks, knives and spoons are held by their handles so no fingerprints are left, and polished with a clean cloth.
polishing
Carrying a tray
The tray is balanced on the fingertips and palm of the left hand. Heavy items go in the middle, at the tray's centre.
balance
Hygiene
Service staff must also receive hygiene training. Glasses are not held by the rim, plates not by the eating surface.
hygiene training
Busser
The waiter's assistant: prepares tables, serves bread and water, clears empty plates and learns by watching.
busser

Rules of service
From which side?
Which side you serve from depends on the type of service. In plated service, plates are usually placed and cleared from the guest's right.
service side
Drinks
Drinks are served from the guest's right, the side where the glass stands.
drink service
Order
Usually guests, older people and children are served first; the host of the table is served last.
order of service
Hot and cold
Hot food goes on a hot plate, cold food on a cold plate. A plate waiting in the kitchen is taken out without delay.
plate temperature
Quiet clearing
Plates are cleared when everyone at the table has finished. If the cutlery lies parallel on the plate, the guest has finished.
"finished" signal
Never
Never reach across in front of a guest, never stack plates on the table while clearing, never hold a glass by its rim.
don'ts

Serving drinks
A guest asks for tea. What do you ask?
"Strong or light?"
"How many glasses will you drink?"
Nothing, I just bring it
"In a glass or a mug?"
Not everyone drinks tea the same way. Asking strong or light is a small touch guests notice right away.
How is a tea glass placed on the table?
Without a saucer, straight on the table
On its saucer, spoon on the saucer, to the guest's right
Held by the rim, into the guest's hand
To the guest's left, spoon inside the glass
Tea comes on its saucer with the spoon on it. Drinks are served from the guest's right; never hold a glass by the rim.
You've brought a bottle of wine to the table. What do you do before opening it?
Open it in the kitchen and bring it
Show the label to the guest who ordered and confirm it's the right wine
Fill everyone's glass straight away
Leave the bottle on the table for them to open
Show the label and open the bottle in front of the guest. The person who ordered gets a small taste first; once they approve, serve the others and them last.
How full is a wine glass poured?
To the brim
Usually between a third and a half
A few drops
Until the guest says stop
Leave room in the glass so the wine can breathe and its aroma comes through; a full glass also spills easily.

Nothing, it comes the standard way
Single or double, and how they want water and ice
Their age
What they'll eat
Rakı is drunk to personal taste: single or double, with water and ice brought separately and added as the guest likes.
A table's water glasses are almost empty. What do you do?
Wait until they ask
Notice it and offer to refill
Clear the glasses
Open a new bottle and leave it on the table
A good waiter notices before being asked. Refill from the guest's right while the glass stays on the table.

Tea: ask strong or light, bring it on the saucer.
Wine: show the label, open it in front of them, offer a taste.
Don't overfill glasses, never hold them by the rim.
Spot empty glasses before anyone asks.
A safe dining room
Accidents in the dining room happen in a second. Tap each action: right or wrong?
Right
Wrong
Sweeping up broken glass with a brush and dustpan
Glass cuts hands. Use a brush and dustpan and put it in a separate, labelled container.
Quickly picking up broken glass by hand
Never use your hands to save time; tiny shards are invisible and cut.
Putting a warning sign on a wet floor
Slipping is the most common accident in a dining room. Sign first, then dry it at once.
Calling "Behind you!" when passing someone
If someone with a tray turns suddenly, you collide. A short warning prevents it.
Holding a hot plate with a service cloth and warning "The plate is hot"
It protects both your hand and the guest.
Running with a full tray when it's busy
Walk fast but never run. A dropped tray means an accident and lost time.
Putting spare chairs in front of the emergency exit
Emergency exits and routes must always stay clear.
Calling 112 for a guest who feels unwell and informing the head waiter
In a serious case, call 112 first. If someone on the team has first-aid training, fetch them at once.
Telling a guest whose lips swell after eating "It'll pass"
This can be an allergic reaction and get worse fast. Call 112 and inform the head waiter.
Pushing the door open with your back while carrying a tray
Keep the tray in front and open the door with your back; follow the kitchen's in and out door rule.
A safe dining room
Broken glass: brush and dustpan, never hands.
Wet floor: sign first, then dry.
Walk fast, don't run; call out when passing behind.
Illness or allergy signs: call 112.
Busser at lunch service
13:00, the dining room is full. You're helping a waiter.
You have full glasses on your tray and a child is running in your path.
I stop, wait for the child to pass, then walk on
No rushing with a tray; safety comes first.
I speed up and pass in front of them
A collision puts both the child and the tray at risk.
I shout "Move!"
You never speak to a guest like that, especially a child.
A guest: "Could I have some water?" But this table isn't in your section.
I say "I'll bring it right away", bring the water and let the waiter know
Guests don't know about sections; the team is one restaurant.
I say "Your waiter will come"
Turning down a small request keeps the guest waiting.
I pretend I didn't hear
Being ignored is what annoys guests most.
At one table, one of three people is still eating and two have finished.
I wait until everyone has finished
Plates are usually cleared when everyone has finished; the person still eating doesn't feel rushed.
I clear the finished plates right away
The last person eating feels pressured.
I clear them all so the table is empty
A plate isn't taken before the guest finishes their meal.
A good busser
Don't rush with a tray.
Every guest is your guest.
Plates are cleared when everyone has finished.

Taking orders

Dinner service
Friday evening, there are five tables in your section.
Guest: "I didn't order this!" You check the ticket: the mistake is yours.
I apologise, ask for the right dish right away, and ask the head waiter whether we can offer something while they wait
Admitting the mistake and solving it quickly wins the guest back.
I say "That's what you said"
Blaming the guest when the mistake is yours loses them.
I say "Eat this, it's basically the same"
The dish the guest wanted must be brought.
You accidentally spilled water on a guest.
I apologise immediately, bring a clean napkin and tell the head waiter
A quick, calm response turns the accident into a small memory.
I walk away as if I hadn't seen
Running away leaves a worse impression than the accident.
I wipe the guest down myself with a napkin
You don't touch a guest without permission; you hand them a napkin.
You see a line on the bill saying "service charge 10%", and the guest asks about it.

I say "That's our rule"

I say "It's instead of a tip"

Evening rules
If the mistake is yours, apologise and fix it.
In an accident, stay calm and help.
No mandatory service charge; tips are voluntary.
The bill at the table
Dinner service is winding down. You're taking payment from your tables.
Four friends: "Can we pay separately?"
I say "Of course" and split the bill item by item from the order
That's exactly why orders are written by seat: everyone pays for what they had.
I say "We can't split it, one bill only"
Refusing a doable request loses guests. Unless there's a house rule, help them.
I divide the total by four and give everyone the same amount
People who ask to pay separately want to pay for their own food. Split equally only if they ask.
The guest will pay by card.
I take the card to the till
The card should never leave the guest's sight; it's about trust and security.
I bring the card machine to the table and the guest enters the PIN
Right. Look away while they type the PIN, and never ask for it.
I ask for the PIN and type it in myself
A PIN is private; a waiter never asks for it.
Another table pays cash: 1,000 TL for a 650 TL bill.
I assume the change is a tip and don't bring it
Tips are the guest's decision. Change is always brought back.
I bring back 350 TL change with the receipt and count it in front of the guest
Counting in front of them avoids misunderstandings. A receipt or invoice for every sale is a legal requirement.
I say "No change" and bring back 300 TL
You can't short a guest. If there's no change, get it from the head waiter or the till.
Guest: "No need for a receipt, keep it."
I still issue the receipt and leave it with the guest
Issuing a receipt is the business's legal duty; it's issued even if the guest doesn't want it.
I don't issue one, it saves paper
Not issuing a receipt can count as tax evasion and leads to fines for the business.
I give the order slip instead of a receipt
The order slip is an internal record; it doesn't replace the legal receipt.
The guests are getting up to leave.
I remind them "You didn't leave a tip"
Tips are voluntary; asking or hinting is wrong.
I thank them, say we hope to see them again, and check the table for forgotten items
The last impression matters as much as the first. If a phone or keys are left behind, you catch them at once.
I start clearing the table at once
Clearing before guests are out the door sends a "please leave" message.

Responsible alcohol service

Alcohol may not be sold or served to anyone under 18. This also applies to a teenager sitting at an adults' table.
